entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on cancer systems biology and combines experimental, computational and AI methods to improve cancer diagnosis, treatment and early detection. Its main themes are modeling how tumors evolve, linking genetic changes to malignant traits, and developing biomarkers to guide treatment decisions. Current members work on early cancer evolution (for example Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia), tissue ecology in ER+ breast cancer using single-cell spatial transcriptomics, and AI/ML for spatial multiomics and computational pathology. I could not open the individual research pages, so the specific methods listed here come from the main page and the members' own focus descriptions.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps strongly on cancer genomics, computational and ML methods, and single-cell and spatial omics. Structural variants and bulk WGS or transcriptome work are less clearly emphasized on the pages I could access. The lab is in the US, so the student may need a visa.

flags: The old Stanford lab page (med.stanford.edu/curtislab) says the lab moved to curtis-lab.com, so the new site is the current one.
No email addresses are published on the members page.
The members page does not give a date or years in program, so I could not tell how current it is.

The page lists clinical fellows (Marni McClure, Audris Chiang, Colin Bergstrom, Zach Ziheng Xu), a post-baccalaureate researcher (Jimmy Zhang) and a medical student (Sophia Pribus). I left them out as not postdocs or PhD students.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab pairs experimental biology with computational methods to study human disease at the molecular level, mainly metastatic cancer and neurodegenerative disease. Its computational work includes AI/ML models for genomics. A second thread is cancer evolution and tumour-environment interactions. A third is post-transcriptional gene regulation, including RNA biology in metastasis. The lab recruits computational biology, RNA biology and cancer postdocs, and takes students from UCSF's Tetrad, BMS, BMI and IPQB programs.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's interests in cancer genomics and ML methods for genomics, but its emphasis is RNA regulation and wet-lab/AI work. Structural variants, somatic mutation analysis and WGS are not evident themes, and the US location would likely need a visa.

flags: The PI is dual-affiliated: Arc Core Investigator since 2023 and still at UCSF, so this is not a full move. goodarzilab.ucsf.edu/people redirects to the Arc homepage.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies mutational signatures, which are the patterns of somatic mutation left in genomes by endogenous and environmental processes. They develop computational methods to find and attribute these signatures across single-base substitutions, indels, copy number and structural variation. They apply these methods to large cancer whole-genome and exome cohorts and to normal tissues, including clonal hematopoiesis and exposure-related mutagenesis. Other work includes duplex sequencing to detect rare mutations, APOBEC mutagenesis, machine learning integration, deep learning on histopathology slides, and signature-based biomarkers for therapy and tumour evolution.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in cancer whole-genome sequencing, somatic mutation and structural variant analysis, and computational and ML methods. There is little single-cell or spatial omics work, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab does cancer genome analysis. It looks for somatic events that drive cancer or resistance to therapy, and for germline risk variants. It uses these to define disease subtypes and link them to clinical outcomes. It builds analysis tools and pipelines for large national and international cancer genome projects, and it has a large engineering and staff-scientist group alongside its trainees. Current work, from the roster and 2026 job postings, includes multiple myeloma initiation, progression and relapse, spatial multi-omics, structural variation patterns, and immunotherapy and CAR-T resistance in lymphoma, using whole-genome/exome and transcriptome sequencing and statistical and machine-learning models.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps strongly on cancer WGS/transcriptome analysis, somatic mutation and structural variant methods, ML, and spatial omics. The main hurdle is that a US visa would be needed.

entries.name: Ding Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on computational cancer genomics. It integrates large-scale multi-omic data, including whole-genome and exome sequencing, RNA-seq, proteomics, single-cell and single-nucleus sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics. It is a long-standing member of consortium efforts such as TCGA and CPTAC. It also works on cellular senescence and aging (SenNet), using organoid, PDX and mouse models together with imaging and AI-based computational pathology. The lab's code is on GitHub (ding-lab). entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab aims to build an AI-driven model of the cell that can turn a patient's data into precision diagnosis and treatment. Its main approach is mapping cellular and disease networks, using protein-interaction and multi-scale cell-structure maps. It has also mapped genetic interactions, including synthetic-lethal maps made with CRISPR/Cas9. It develops the Cytoscape network analysis software and leads large programs: the Cancer Cell Map Initiative, the NIH Bridge2AI Cell Maps for AI project, and the ARPA-H ADAPT 'digital tumors' project for precision oncology. Methods combine interpretable machine learning on biological hierarchies, tumour genomics and imaging, and network biology.

entries.department_hint: Innovation Investigator, Arc Institute; Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering, Stanford
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning models of biological sequence and evolution, with the aim of aligning biological AI with human good. It studies how the immune system balances short-term protection with long-term adaptability, in order to inform more robust therapeutics. It also builds evolutionary and generative genome language models, such as Evo 2, to design new proteins, genes, antibodies and bacteriophage genomes. A third area is safe biological AI: generative models that help researchers counter harmful biology. The work is mostly computational and focuses on model development and design, not on cancer or clinical genomics.

entries.name: Palotie Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the genetic basis of common neurological, neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric diseases, including migraine, epilepsy and schizophrenia, along with their comorbidities and some cardiovascular traits. It uses clinical and population samples from the Finnish founder population. Its methods are genome-wide association studies, sequencing studies, and family-based designs. The group exploits population bottlenecks to find low-frequency and rare variants. Palotie is also Scientific Director/Chief Scientific Officer of the FinnGen biobank-scale project. The group's published description does not mention cancer.

entries.name: Klein Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops technologies and computational methods to study how cells make fate decisions in development and disease. It is known for high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics (inDrop) and for computational analysis of cell state and lineage dynamics. Current work includes semi-permeable CAGE capsules for multi-step single-cell genomic analysis and live-cell functional screening, and genomics tools for mapping the niche and signaling landscapes that determine stem-cell self-renewal and fate. It also covers microbial functional genomics and perturbational transcriptomics in bacteria, cross-species transcriptomics, and single-cell tracking of differentiation.

entries.name: Segre Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and statistical genetics methods to find the genetic and biological causes of common eye diseases, including age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. Most polygenic disease associations fall in noncoding regions. The lab therefore integrates epigenomic data, eQTLs and transcriptomes with genome-wide association and sequencing studies, and uses them to fine-map noncoding signals and to run pathway analyses of rare and common variants. Other directions are pharmacogenomics of adverse ocular drug responses, drug repurposing and adverse-effect prediction through cross-trait genetic analyses, and links between rare and common retinal degeneration. The lab also contributes to the GTEx and single-cell atlas work, including a multi-tissue cell atlas.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational and functional genomics methods with the student's interests, but it studies germline genetics of eye disease. It has no cancer, tumour sequencing or structural-variant focus, and a US role would need a visa.

entries.focus: The group develops computational and AI methods to analyze how genetics and environment jointly shape health and disease. Core work is exposome research, including leading the NEXUS network (Network for Exposomics in the United States). A meta-science strand studies the robustness of big-data findings, using the 'vibration of effects' approach.

entries.focus: The lab uses machine learning to interpret genetic variation and to design biological molecules. It has three areas: (1) learning the 'language of life', which uses evolutionary couplings between co-mutating amino acids to study protein and RNA structure and function; (2) predicting the effects of single and combined mutations and designing stable, functional protein sequences; and (3) viral evolution and immunology, which predicts viral escape and pathogenicity, improves immune recognition and identifies antibody targets. Current members also work on T-cell receptor and antibody models, immune repertoires, enzyme and protein dynamics, and interpretable ML for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. The lab's tagline is 'Machine learning to accelerate biology'.

entries.name: Robinson Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies genetic influences on behaviour and cognition, with an emphasis on neurodevelopmental variation and on differences within and between neuropsychiatric disorders. It uses statistical genetics and epidemiology to study common and rare genetic risk factors for severe neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism and ADHD. It develops quantitative methods to link these risk factors to behaviour and cellular biology. Funded projects include ADHD and developmental-disorder epidemiology and genetics in Kenya and South Africa. This is human population and psychiatric genetics, not cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The lab does statistical and psychiatric genetics (autism, ADHD, neurodevelopment) and has no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural-variant, or single-cell/spatial work. The only overlap is general computational genetics methods.

entries.name: Rheinbay Lab
entries.focus: The lab identifies and functionally characterizes non-coding driver mutations in tumour whole-genome sequences. It does this mainly by developing new computational analysis methods and collaborating with experimental groups. A second theme is breast and prostate cancer genomics and epigenomics, including the FOXA1 oncogene and its regulatory-element and 3' UTR mutations. A third theme is the role of the sex chromosomes in cancer, especially loss of the Y chromosome (LOY). The lab is building specialized tools to define Y chromosome status in tumours, which is hard because the chromosome is repetitive. The PI co-led the PCAWG non-coding driver analysis of 2,658 whole genomes (Nature, 2020).

fit.reason: The lab's work on tumour whole-genome somatic mutation analysis and computational method development matches the student's core interests, but I saw no evidence of single-cell/spatial or transcriptome-focused work, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Macosko Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops genomics technologies to study brain diseases, especially schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease. It builds high-throughput single-cell and spatial methods, including Drop-seq, Slide-seq and Slide-tags. The lab applies them to identify new brain cell types, cellular responses to psychological stress, and neurons that are vulnerable to neurodegeneration.

entries.focus: The lab develops tools that combine single-cell genomics with spatial and temporal information. Applications include tissue development and regeneration, and how tissue organization breaks down in injury and disease. These include cancer evolution and the tumour microenvironment.

entries.name: Michor Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer evolution: how tumours initiate, progress, respond to therapy and develop resistance. It builds computational methods from applied mathematics, statistics, bioinformatics, machine learning and AI. It also integrates experimental, clinical and population-science data. fit.reason: The lab overlaps on computational and ML methods and on single-cell and spatial cancer omics, but its core is evolutionary and mathematical modelling, with little emphasis on WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation calling.

entries.name: Getz Lab (Cancer Genome Computational Analysis)
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies computational methods to characterize genomic events in cancer, including somatic mutations, copy-number changes and structural variants, and how they drive clonal evolution. Current interests are tumor heterogeneity, single-cell and spatial analysis of tumors and their microenvironment, drivers of therapy resistance, proteogenomics, and somatic mutations in normal tissues. The group also builds widely used analysis software and cloud pipelines, and runs large-scale cancer genome projects. Job postings show active work on multiple myeloma and spatial multi-omics.

entries.name: Lahav Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how biological signals change over time in human cells, with a main focus on the tumour suppressor p53 and how it drives cell-fate decisions after DNA damage. Its methods are live imaging of fluorescently tagged proteins in single cells, phenotypic and statistical analysis, and mathematical modelling. The aim is to understand p53 regulation and function, from molecular to organismal levels, in normal physiology and in cancer. The work is mostly cell-line dynamics and quantitative systems biology. It is not sequencing-based genomics.

fit.reason: The lab is cancer-related and quantitative, with single-cell methods and modelling, but it does little tumour WGS, structural-variant or somatic-mutation work. Its single-cell work is live-cell imaging, not single-cell or spatial omics.

Its current work centres on scalable inference methods and modelling for single-cell genomic data and in situ imaging data. A particular emphasis is on how tumours and the immune system co-evolve. The work is largely computational, combining statistical and machine-learning methods with mathematical modelling of tumour and disease evolution. This page does not describe specific cancer types or datasets, so the finer detail comes from the PI's publications, which I did not review.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in computational methods and ML for cancer genomics and in single-cell and spatial omics; there is less visible emphasis on bulk WGS/transcriptome and structural-variant analysis, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Buenrostro Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how cells acquire and reverse epigenetic changes and how those changes contribute to disease. It builds on ATAC-seq and extends it to single-cell assays (scATAC-seq, dsciATAC-seq, SHARE-seq) and to spatial genome mapping (IGS, ExIGS, slide-DNA-seq). It develops machine-learning models trained on epigenomic data to infer cell composition and function and to predict cell fate. It also studies epigenetic memory of inflammation and its link to cancer priming, and uses social-adversity models to study how stress affects the epigenome, immune and endocrine systems, and aging. A further goal is population-scale epigenomic sequencing with biobanks.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with single-cell and spatial omics and with computational and ML methods for genomics, but the lab focuses on chromatin and epigenomics, adversity and aging, with little on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation, and a US role may need a visa.

The work is human-genomics and statistical-genetics based, with international collaborations. It does not study cancer.

entries.name: Daly Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods to find and interpret genetic variation in complex disease. entries.name: Bulyk Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies transcriptional gene regulation, in particular how transcription factors (TFs) recognize DNA and how that recognition shapes regulatory element activity. Its main methods are high-throughput in vitro assays of protein-DNA binding, such as protein binding microarrays, together with computational modelling of TF binding specificity. It also uses massively parallel reporter assays and related functional genomics to test how non-coding variants and regulatory sequences affect gene expression. The lab applies these approaches to human disease-associated non-coding variation. Recent work includes a 2025 Nature paper on how multiple overlapping binding sites determine TF occupancy. This summary draws on the lab's listed postdoc topics and on the 2025 Nature paper, not on a fetched research page.

entries.name: Hemberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and statistical methods for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. Current methods work covers spatial statistics for tissue organisation, a next-generation Harmony for batch correction that scales to tens of millions of cells, and Scotia, which infers cell-cell communication from spatial data. A further line of work builds liquid-biopsy methods that detect tumour-derived RNA in blood for early cancer detection. Collaborative applications include pancreatic cancer treatment resistance (Hwang lab), CAR T-cell response in solid tumours, influenza vaccine response, and perianal fistulizing disease. The lab was at the Wellcome Sanger Institute from 2014 to 2021.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interest in computational methods and single-cell/spatial omics in cancer (pancreatic cancer, liquid-biopsy RNA, CAR-T tumours), but there is little focus on whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation calling.

entries.name: Meyerson Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses genomic approaches to find the causes of human cancers and turn those findings into therapies. It uses whole-genome sequencing to study DNA changes inside and outside the coding genome, including enhancer rearrangements that change gene expression, and long-read sequencing of structural variants. Lung cancer work covers kinase signaling, splicing-factor mutations (such as U2AF1), inflammatory signaling and aneuploidy. entries.name: Baym Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies microbial evolution through experiment, computation and theory. A central question is how selection acts on mobile genetic elements (plasmids, transposons, prophages) and their bacterial hosts, at the scales of the cell, between cells and across populations. Antibiotic resistance is a major theme. Methods include synthetic lab evolution systems, large-scale analysis of clinical and environmental sequencing data, and new algorithms and technologies (for example, earlier work on compressive genomics and sequence-search methods). The PI's profile also mentions using ancient DNA and strain archives to study bacteria from before clinical antibiotic use.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational and sequence-analysis methods with the student's interests, but it works on bacterial evolution and antibiotic resistance, not cancer genomics, structural variants, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Springer Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how evolution shapes and constrains the way organisms respond to their environment. It also asks how biochemistry, molecular design and regulatory wiring let cells process environmental information. The lab compares related yeast species and duplicated genes, and currently focuses on pH homeostasis. Methods include in vivo fluorescence, synthetic and genetic approaches, and numerical and analytical modeling. The lab has also been involved in COVID-19 testing work.

entries.name: Talkowski Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genomic variation, especially structural variation (SV), contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism. They build population-scale SV resources, including the Structural Variation Atlas, the GATK-SV pipeline, and long-read gnomAD, and map complex genomic rearrangements. They run large gene-discovery and disease-association studies in autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders, including rare-disease and bipolar cohorts. They use cellular and functional modeling (iPSC-derived neural models, high-throughput variant-to-function assays, long-read RNA-seq and splicing) to interpret variants. They also work on translational prenatal and pediatric genomic diagnostics.

fit.reason: The lab's SV calling, long-read analysis and ML/statistical genomics methods overlap strongly with the student's interest in structural variants and computational methods, but its focus is germline neurodevelopmental disease rather than cancer, somatic mutation, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spat

entries.name: Udler Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics to improve diagnosis and treatment of diabetes and metabolic disease. It builds partitioned polygenic scores and clusters genetic loci into mechanism-specific groups to explain heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes. A 2024 Nature Medicine paper from the lab did this in more than 1.4 million people across ancestries. It also leads MGH recruitment for the RADIANT study of rare and atypical diabetes, using sequencing to find new genes and variants. Data sources are large biobanks (UK Biobank, Mass General Brigham Biobank, the T2D Knowledge Portal). Methods are statistical genetics, GWAS and polygenic scores, multi-omics, and pharmacogenomics, alongside a clinical Diabetes Genetics Clinic.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational and statistical-genomics methods with the student, but it works on germline genetics of diabetes and metabolic disease rather than cancer, tumour WGS/transcriptomes, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Hacohen Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds systems-biology tools to model immune processes at the cellular and molecular level. It uses genome-wide genetic screens in primary immune cells, for example work showing that STING acts as a proton channel. It also does single-cell and spatial profiling to define immune cell types and disease-associated cell states, including in sepsis, lupus nephritis and tumour immunity, and it contributes to the Human Cell Atlas. A translational arm develops personalized neoantigen cancer vaccines and machine-learning methods for predicting cancer antigens, and the lab models human immune diseases in mice.

fit.reason: Single-cell/spatial tumour immune profiling and ML neoantigen prediction overlap with the student's computational cancer interests, but the lab is immunology-centred rather than focused on WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation calling, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.name: Rigollet Lab
entries.focus: The group works at the interface of statistics, machine learning and optimization, with a focus on high-dimensional statistical methods. One theme models transformers as interacting particle systems, where self-attention acts as a velocity field that moves tokens, and studies the resulting clustering behaviour. A second theme applies Wasserstein gradient flows and optimal transport to statistics and ML, including particle-based variational inference and nonparametric maximum likelihood. A third theme applies transformers and probability-measure methods to biological data, treating cell populations as probability measures, for example to predict treatment response in patient-derived organoids. The group does this work with the Schmidt Center at the Broad Institute and is recruiting postdocs on maths-biology and genomics.

entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational methods for large-scale human genetics, working mainly with biobank data such as the UK Biobank. Related work covers phasing, imputation, and polygenic and mixed-model association methods.

Other themes are tumour evolution and comparison of primary and metastatic tumours.

entries.name: Hormoz Lab
entries.focus: The lab asks how biological history shapes future cell fate. It studies how distinct cell states arise in viruses, bacteria and mammalian cells, and how to produce desired cell states in a dish, for example blood stem cells from fibroblasts or embryonic stem cells. Because high-throughput measurements destroy cells, it engineers cells that record their lineage and signaling histories in their own DNA, and it develops cell barcoding with in situ readout alongside transcriptomes. It also uses directed viral evolution for gene delivery, and gastruloid and organoid models of early human development. Analysis relies on differential geometry, machine learning, population genetics and stochastic processes, including reconstructing the origins and clonal expansion of blood cancers in individual patients.

entries.name: Naqvi Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how quantitative control of gene expression shapes development and the 'tipping points' that lead to disease. It focuses on transcription factor (TF) dosage. It uses chemical-genetic approaches to modulate TF levels in fine increments in human stem cells and their derived cell types, such as neural crest. The lab pairs these perturbations with functional genomics and builds predictive computational and machine learning models of the molecular, cellular and morphological effects. The PI's earlier work covered cis-regulatory divergence between human and chimpanzee, and sex-biased gene expression in mammals.

entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (experimental plus computational genomics)
entries.focus: The lab studies how long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate gene expression and organize the nucleus in 3D. A major model is Xist and X-chromosome silencing. Xist finds its targets through 3D proximity, spreads by remodeling X-chromosome structure, and recruits SHARP/SMRT/HDAC3 to exclude RNA Polymerase II. The lab also proposes a 'seed, bind, recruit' model, in which hundreds of ncRNAs form nuclear compartments that concentrate RNA-binding proteins, and it examines the role of phase separation. Methods include SPRITE (mapping RNA, DNA and protein assemblies in 3D at single-molecule resolution), RNA-protein interaction profiling, CRISPRi screens, single-cell transcriptomics, and microscopy. Other work covers SARS-CoV-2 protein interactions with host RNAs.

fit.reason: This is mostly experimental RNA and nuclear-architecture biology, with some single-cell and genomic method development. It has little cancer genomics, tumour WGS, structural-variant or somatic-mutation work, so overlap with the student's interests is limited, and it would involve a US visa.

entries.name: O'Connor Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and mathematical methods to characterize the genetic architecture of common diseases and traits. One thread quantifies how common and rare variants contribute to disease risk, how natural selection shapes that architecture, and how functional annotations can be integrated. This includes work on autism and forecasts of what rare-variant association studies will find at larger sample sizes. A second thread builds methods that use genealogical relatedness (shared haplotypes from common ancestors). It includes a genealogical representation of the linkage disequilibrium (LD) matrix that speeds up calculations such as heritability partitioning, and a similar representation for genotype data. The work is population-genetic and statistical, centred on GWAS and rare-variant data. It does not cover tumour sequencing, somatic mutation, or single-cell and spatial omics.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and statistical methods for genomics, but it works on germline common and rare variants in complex traits. It does no cancer, somatic, structural-variant, or single-cell and spatial work, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods to study how spatial organization relates to normal and diseased cell states. Other Aryee work I saw only in secondary sources includes statistical methods for cancer epigenetics and safer CRISPR and genome-editing tools.

Methods include synthetic lab evolution systems, large-scale analysis of clinical and environmental sequencing data, and new technologies.

entries.name: Gehlenborg Lab (HIDIVE)
entries.focus: The lab builds interactive visualization and analysis tools that help scientists and clinicians explore complex biomedical data. Its open-source software includes HiGlass (genome/Hi-C browsing), Gosling (a grammar for genomics visualization), and Vitessce (single-cell and spatial data). Application areas include cancer genomics (for example TCGA data visualization), epigenomics and 3D genome organization, and single-cell and spatial atlases such as HuBMAP, SenNet and KPMP. Methods combine human-computer interaction, visualization research, and software engineering for reproducible, collaborative data analysis.

entries.focus: The lab builds medical AI that reasons from evidence, tests it before it is trusted, and teaches it to assist clinicians. The lab mixes computer scientists and clinicians, and the work centres on medical imaging and clinical-record AI.

entries.name: Keating Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how proteins bind each other in eukaryotic signaling, and it combines computational modeling with experiments to do so. A major thread is Bcl-2 family proteins that control apoptosis. Structure-based and machine-learning models predict BH3 motif binding, and these models have produced peptide reagents for assessing programmed cell death in cancer cells. Newer projects cover short linear motif recognition by domains such as TRAF, EVH1 and the E3 ligase Itch. The lab also designs peptide binders and inhibitors, including cyclotides and conformationally pre-organized peptides. Methods include yeast surface display, photo-crosslinking, and machine learning for sequence–structure–energy landscapes.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in machine learning methods and touches cancer biology through apoptosis, but it works on protein structure and peptide design, not genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Bryson Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines immunoengineering, molecular microbiology, and synthetic and systems biology to design new therapeutics for infectious disease. Its main focus is Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the role of the human innate immune system, especially macrophages, in controlling infection. It builds tools to study infection from single cells to whole infected animals, using quantitative modeling with classical microbiology and immunology methods. The two central questions are which macrophage processes kill bacteria and how the bacteria resist them, and how macrophage plasticity can be manipulated to program function. The long-term goal is to inform TB vaccine design.

entries.focus: The group works at the intersection of AI and chemistry. It builds machine learning models of how molecules behave, interact and react, and uses them to design new molecules, with an emphasis on therapeutic discovery. Topics include computer-aided synthesis planning and retrosynthesis, reaction outcome and mechanism prediction, generative models for small-molecule and 3D structure-based drug design, and structure elucidation from mass spectrometry and metabolomics data. The group also uses laboratory automation and high-throughput experimentation to test hypotheses and generate data, for example in catalyst design and nanoparticle cancer therapeutics.

entries.name: Page Lab
entries.focus: The Page lab studies how genetic differences between males and females arise and what they mean for biology and medicine, both inside and outside the reproductive tract. It uses comparative, evolutionary, developmental and clinical approaches. The lab sequenced the sex chromosomes of eight mammals and chicken, and found Y-linked genes with X-linked counterparts that are expressed throughout the body. It now studies how XX versus XY chromosome makeup shapes genome-wide sex differences in gene expression and disease, using genomic, proteomic and epigenetic profiling. It also develops methods for high-quality sequencing of complex genomic regions, and uses mouse models of germ cell development, with implications for infertility and germ cell cancers.

fit.reason: The lab is strong in genomics and computational analysis, but its focus is sex-chromosome biology and germ cells, not cancer genomics, structural variants in tumours or single-cell/spatial cancer omics (only a minor link through germ cell cancers). Joining would also need a US visa.

Other topics include nuclear organization and mechanics, epigenetic memory through mitosis and cell fate, the 3D structure of sister chromatids, and the role of non-coding RNAs in chromatin organization. The lab also builds computational tools, including Bayesian inference of loop extrusion and the machine-learning tool Manta.

entries.name: Lieberman Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how bacterial strains evolve and colonize within complex communities, with the human skin microbiome as the main model. It infers within-person bacterial evolution from cultured isolates and whole-genome data, using new computational and statistical methods that do not need longitudinal studies. The aim is to predict which strains can stably colonize a person and how personalized microbial communities relate to skin disease. The results are meant to help design more precise microbiome-based therapies.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational whole-genome sequencing and mutation-calling methods with the student's interests, but it works on bacterial microbiome evolution, not cancer genomics, structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning models trained on large-scale microbial genomic and metagenomic data to discover and design new microbial functions. Its four research areas are molecular interactions and cellular function, microbial biochemistry (enzyme and pathway discovery, generative design of biosynthetic systems), microbial technologies (natural products, biomanufacturing, therapeutics), and microbial ecology and evolution. Methods include genomic language models that reason over genomic context, generative design, sequence-variation analysis, and experimental engineering and validation. The lab works on microbial genomes, not human or cancer genomics.

entries.name: Cardona Group (connectomics)
entries.focus: The group does experimental and comparative connectomics. It maps synaptic wiring diagrams of small brains, mainly the larval fruit fly (Drosophila), and also other small animals across the animal phylogenetic tree, using volume electron microscopy. The work has moved from sensory and motor circuits to deeper regions such as the mushroom body (memory) and the central complex (spatial learning and motor planning). Methods combine EM reconstruction, behavioural analysis, electrophysiology and optophysiology, open-source image-analysis software, and computational circuit models that link connectivity to behaviour. Recent computational work includes analyses of synaptic density and wiring optimisation across species.

fit.reason: The lab works on neural circuit connectomics and EM image analysis, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is generic computational and ML methods.

entries.name: Murshudov Group (Computational structural biology)
entries.focus: The group develops mathematical, statistical and computational methods for building reliable atomic models from noisy, incomplete experimental data, with a focus on automation. It uses Bayesian frameworks that combine crystallography and cryo-EM data with prior stereochemical and structural knowledge. Its software includes REFMAC5, AceDRG, ProSMART, EMDA, LIBG, Servalcat and MetalCoord. Paul Emsley, who is listed on the group page, leads development of Coot (model building and validation) and the web-based Moorhen.

entries.name: Greener Group (biomolecular simulation / force fields)
entries.focus: The group works on improving force fields for biomolecular simulation. They train molecular mechanics force fields with graph neural networks, quantum mechanics data and experimental data, and they work toward a universal biomolecular force field. They also develop fast machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for biomolecules, with the long-term aim of simulating enzyme reactions. Other projects include reactive force fields, protein design using molecular simulation, protein folding and free energy methods. The group builds differentiable molecular simulation software, including Molly.jl in Julia.

fit.reason: The group does biomolecular physics and force-field development, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is the general use of machine learning methods.

entries.focus: The group studies how animals store learned behaviours in neural circuits and retrieve them. The zebra finch is the main model, because adult birds sing songs they practised as juveniles. A songbird basal ganglia connectome dataset with over 8,500 neurons was released in 2025.

entries.name: Scheres Group (cryo-EM computational methods, RELION)
entries.focus: The group develops cryo-EM and cryo-ET image-processing methods, implemented in the open-source RELION package. Current method work includes deep-learning priors and more efficient optimisation algorithms for reconstruction, and machine-learning applications to cryo-ET. On the biology side, the group determines cryo-EM structures of amyloid filaments (especially tau) extracted from human brain, often with Michel Goedert's group, to link filament folds to specific neurodegenerative diseases. It also reproduces these folds with in vitro assembly of tau and other amyloids to study the mechanisms behind disease-specific folds.

fit.reason: The lab works on structural biology and cryo-EM methods for neurodegeneration, with some machine-learning methods work. It has no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural-variant or single-cell/spatial omics work, so overlap with the student's interests is limited to general ML/computational methods.

entries.name: Landau Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies somatic evolution: how single cells accumulate mutations over a lifetime and how the resulting clonal expansions affect health and cancer. It uses genotype-aware single-cell multiomics on human samples. This compares mutant and wild-type cells from the same patient to find mutation-specific phenotypes. It also does whole-genome sequencing of cell-free plasma DNA for liquid biopsy, aiming to detect circulating tumour DNA at parts-per-million fractions without a matched tumour sample. A third line of work is human single-cell lineage tracing, which builds somatic phylogenies from intrinsic genetic barcodes together with phenotyping. The lab combines computational and experimental tools to study cancer evolution and to design precision-medicine approaches that overcome it.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with single-cell cancer omics, computational methods and WGS-based cfDNA and somatic mutation analysis; it is less centred on structural variants or tumour transcriptome profiling, and a US visa would be needed.

entries.name: Gürsoy Lab
entries.focus: The lab works at the intersection of computational genomics and privacy/security. It quantifies how much private information leaks from genomic data, including genomic summary results and single-cell RNA-seq data. It also builds software, file formats and pipelines so data can be shared while participants stay protected. A second line of work is 3D genome organization, repeat DNA and regulatory-element evolution. It develops computational methods for how mutations and disease change genome topology and epigenetic patterns. The Cambridge group is broadening into biological encryption, the microbiome and privacy, and statistical genetics with machine learning. Recent postdoc adverts also cover molecular evolution and functional genomics.

fit.reason: Overlap is limited to computational/ML methods for genomics and some single-cell and 3D-genome work, since the lab centres on genome privacy and regulatory genomics rather than cancer genomics, structural variants or somatic mutation, and the move to Cambridge adds a UK visa barrier.

entries.focus: The lab studies the chromosomal structure of DNA in cancer, using cancer genome assembly and long-molecule sequencing (including Pore-C). Main themes are how complex somatic DNA rearrangements, such as those involving genome graphs and extrachromosomal DNA, shape the tumour epigenome. The lab also uses structural variation to infer mutational processes in somatic evolution from pre-cancer to metastasis. It translates this work into clinical-grade whole-genome analysis tools, including the Genome Oncology System (gOS) at NYU Langone, for genomic diagnostics and precision oncology.

fit.reason: Structural variants, somatic mutation analysis, tumour whole-genome sequencing and computational methods (including machine learning) match the student's core interests closely. The lab has little single-cell or spatial omics work, and a US visa may be needed.

entries.focus: The lab studies how genetic variants in human populations affect gene regulation and molecular and cellular traits, and how those effects contribute to common and rare disease. The focus is germline and population variation, not cancer.

entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods for predicting how biological molecules bind one another and releases them as open-source software. Its current focus is peptide docking with AutoDock CrankPep (ADCP), which folds and docks flexible linear and cyclic peptides. The lab is also combining physics-based docking with AI structure predictors such as AlphaFold. Other work covers small-molecule docking, molecular surfaces and visualization, using tools such as MGLTools, MSMS, and the web-based ADapt and WEWoS.

fit.reason: The lab works on structure-based docking and molecular visualization software, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural-variant, or single-cell/spatial omics work, so it overlaps with the student's interests only slightly through general computational methods.

entries.name: Forli Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds computational tools for structure-based drug discovery and uses them on therapeutic targets. A central effort is the AutoDock suite, including GPU-accelerated docking engines, improved force fields and scoring functions, and search algorithms. The lab also works on covalent inhibitor discovery, including proteome-wide ligand discovery with SuFEx chemistry, and on protein flexibility using MD simulations and ensemble docking. Newer work applies machine learning to virtual screening and neural-network force fields (AMOEBA/Tinker-GPU). Many projects are joint with experimental labs and cover membrane proteins, ion channels, neurodegeneration and the unfolded protein response.

fit.reason: The lab does structure-based drug discovery and docking. It has no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural-variant or single-cell/spatial work, so the only overlap with the student's interests is general computational and ML methods. A US visa would also be needed.

entries.focus: The lab combines computational and experimental methods to study how tissues are cellularly organized. It focuses on the diversity and clinical significance of tumour cell subsets and their microenvironments. entries.name: Gentles Lab
entries.focus: The Gentles lab is a computational biology group that analyses large patient cohorts to study human health and disease, mainly cancer and neurodegeneration. A major theme is pan-cancer discovery of prognostic cell types and states. The lab uses CIBERSORTx deconvolution of bulk expression, single-cell RNA-seq and genomic atlases, and it studies how spatial cell organisation shapes tissue behaviour. Another theme is lymph nodes and metastasis, where genomic data and CODEX imaging are used to ask how immune cells come to tolerate migrated tumour cells (Stanford Center for Cancer Systems Biology). A third theme looks for pathways shared between cancer and neurodegeneration, including Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, in collaboration with the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute.

fit.reason: Single-cell/spatial omics in cancer and computational methods overlap well with the student's interests, but the lab works mainly on expression deconvolution and cohort-level analysis rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation calling, and a US role would need a visa.

entries.name: Sidow Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the evolution of function, currently in cancer. Its main program is the evolutionary genomics of cancer, which applies phylogenetic principles to whole-genome sequencing and functional-genomics data from multiple tumour samples taken from the same patient. It develops wet-lab protocols and computational methods for linked-read and long-read nanopore sequencing, aimed at phasing, structural-variant calling and diploid assembly (for example the Aquila assembler). entries.name: Laboratory of Evolutionary Design
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning methods for understanding and designing proteins and genomes. It is best known for the Evo biological foundation model, which does sequence modeling and design from the molecular scale to the genome scale. Its research themes are learning from nature (for example, how the immune system balances short-term protection against long-term adaptability), accelerating evolution by learning evolutionary rules from data, and building safe biological AI. The safe-AI theme includes generative models that let researchers quickly deploy countermeasures against harmful biology. The work is mostly computational, with experimental collaborations.

The approach is mainly clinical informatics and behavioral data science rather than cancer or tumour omics.

entries.name: Alsentzer Lab

entries.name: Pritchard Lab
entries.focus: The lab is mainly computational. It works on statistical genetics, population genetics and ML-based genomics, and has close ties to wet-lab groups. A major theme is linking GWAS and rare-variant results to causal mechanisms, which it calls 'Trait Causal Models'. These models combine genome-scale Perturb-seq and single-cell omics with the omnigenic 'core gene' and trans-regulatory network view of heritability. The work is applied mainly to T cells and immune traits, in collaboration with Alex Marson's lab, and to red blood cell traits. Other work covers QTL mapping and splicing (LeafCutter, WASP), trans-regulation by CRISPR perturbation, population structure and ancient DNA (STRUCTURE, TreeMix), polygenic adaptation and selection, recombination, and the human mutation spectrum.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and ML methods and single-cell work, but it focuses on human complex-trait genetics, population genetics and T-cell regulation. It does little tumour WGS or structural-variant work; the main cancer link is Alvina Adimoelja's population genetics

entries.name: Salzman Lab
entries.focus: The lab treats genomic data as a statistical signal-processing problem. It uses statistics, machine learning and deep learning for biological discovery, with stated interests in splicing, cancer and microbes. A flagship method is SPLASH (and the related NOMAD framework), a reference-free, annotation-free statistical approach that finds sequence variation directly in raw sequencing reads. It is applied to alternative splicing, RNA editing, V(D)J-like diversity, microbial and viral variation, and predictive phenotype models. Cancer-related work includes gene-fusion and circular RNA detection and validation, and new statistical methods for spatial and single-cell sequencing data such as MERFISH isoform analysis.

entries.name: Computational Cancer Biology Group

entries.focus: The lab studies somatic evolution using cancer as a model. One strand asks how mutational processes drive cellular plasticity and stress adaptation, including homologous recombination deficiency in breast cancer and radiotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer. The other strand asks how tumour cells co-evolve with their microenvironment to evade therapy and persist as dormant cells. Methods include statistical modelling, data integration and machine learning across bulk, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics and digital pathology. The group also builds deep learning and foundation-model approaches for multi-omics and H&E images. A UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship funds work on the mutational processes and spatial context of tumour dormancy.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, mutational-process analysis, machine learning for genomics, and single-cell/spatial omics. Overlap on structural variants and tumour WGS is less explicit, and a UK role may need a visa.

The group also reconstructs metastatic migration histories from clinical cohorts such as TRACERx and PEACE research autopsies, and works on glioblastoma initiation and invasion and on prostate cancer genomics with clinical collaborators. Most projects use clinical human samples with a translational goal.

entries.focus: The group studies how somatic mutations and clonal expansions accumulate in normal body cells over an animal's lifetime, and what this means for ageing, cancer and health. The work compares somatic mutation and clonal dynamics across species with different lifespans and body sizes, including long-lived whales, cancer-resistant elephants and primates. A further strand is Peto's Paradox, meaning how large or long-lived species resist cancer. A third strand uses pollutant-linked mutational signatures and clonal changes in sentinel species as early-warning indicators of environmental harm. A 2026 Wellcome grant covers about 30 species, and job ads describe a primate somatic mutation mapping project run with UC Berkeley and the Sanger Institute.

entries.name: Palamara Group (Statistical and Population Genetics)
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and machine learning algorithms to study human genetic variation. The lab releases open-source software for these methods. It received an ERC Consolidator Grant in May 2026 and is advertising an ERC-funded postdoc in statistical machine learning for genomics.

entries.name: Sebé-Pedrós Group
entries.focus: The lab studies how a single genome encodes many cell types and how genome regulation evolves across the tree of life. It uses single-cell genomics to map cell types in whole adult organisms and embryos from diverse animal lineages. It also reconstructs and compares cell-type gene regulatory networks. Its third line combines chromatin profiling and epigenomics to study the evolution of chromatin regulation and genome architecture, from unicellular eukaryotes to animals. It contributes to the Biodiversity Cell Atlas, and the work is heavily computational and comparative.

fit.reason: The lab shares single-cell methods and computational genomics with the student's interests, but it works on evolutionary and developmental biology in non-model organisms, with no cancer, tumour sequencing or somatic variant work.

entries.name: Lehner Group
entries.focus: The group combines large-scale genomics, biophysics, mechanistic modelling and AI to build reference atlases of how DNA sequence changes alter the function of proteins and RNAs. Core topics are protein stability, allostery, sequence-to-affinity and selectivity, amyloids and protein aggregation, RNA splicing and stop codons, and evolution, design and engineering. Methods include deep mutational scanning, mRNA display and proteolysis assays, and machine-learning models trained on the resulting data. Applications include enzyme and antibody design and interpreting human genetic variants for drug discovery.

fit.reason: The lab uses machine learning and computational modelling on genomic variant data, which overlaps with the student's computational methods interest, but it works on protein and RNA variant effects and not on cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Colijn Group
entries.focus: The group works on the mathematics, evolution and epidemiology of infectious pathogens, linking sequence data to infection ecology and evolution. Topics include how co-infection, competition and selection drive antimicrobial resistance, and how genomic data can guide interventions such as resistance control or vaccine strain replacement. The group also does pandemic modelling, including COVID-19 forecasting and genomic epidemiology, for public health bodies. The focus is pathogen genomics, not cancer.

entries.name: Davenport Group
entries.focus: The group integrates functional genomic data with clinical data to understand how human genetics drives patient-to-patient differences in disease severity and treatment response. Much of the work is in immune-mediated and inflammatory conditions such as sepsis, acute infection, lupus and other autoimmune diseases. The group works with clinical and industry partners, with an emphasis on host immune response variation and its relevance to drug development.

fit.reason: The group offers transcriptomics, single-cell analysis and computational genomics methods, but it focuses on germline genetics of immune and infectious disease. It does not cover cancer, tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutations, and a UK role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Meier Group
entries.focus: The group studies speciation and evolutionary genomics. It asks why some lineages speciate far faster than others, and how hybridisation and chromosomal rearrangements (fusions, fissions, translocations, inversions) contribute to rapid speciation and adaptation. It sequences and compares genomes of Ithomiini and Heliconius butterflies, peacock spiders and other insects, and combines these with behavioural and ecological fieldwork. Methods include population genomics, comparative analysis of chromosome-level genomes (Project Psyche, Darwin Tree of Life), structural-variant and breakpoint analysis, and single-cell sperm sequencing. The PI's earlier work on Lake Victoria cichlids showed that hybridisation fuelled adaptive radiations.

entries.focus: The group studies how DNA sequence determines when and where genes are expressed, which it calls the 'Sequence to Expression' problem or the 'second genetic code' of transcription regulation. entries.focus: The group studies somatic mutations, DNA methylation and clonal dynamics in human tissues to understand how clonal selection drives ageing and cancer. entries.name: Google DeepMind
entries.focus: DeepMind's science group builds ML models for biology. AlphaFold predicts protein structure. AlphaGenome reads up to 1 Mb of DNA sequence and predicts 11 genomic processes, including gene expression and splicing, and it scores non-coding regulatory variant effects. It matched or beat the best external models in 25 of 26 variant-effect evaluations. It is available for non-commercial research use, and over 3,000 researchers in 160 countries had used the API by January 2026. Kohli says current work covers protein function, genome interpretation, and de novo protein and enzyme design. DeepMind has also advertised student researcher placements for AI-driven cancer discovery.

Regev's 'lab-in-the-loop' strategy ties experimental data (including large perturbation and single-cell datasets) to ML models that guide the next experiments. Computational Sciences, including the Computational Biology & Medicine centre of excellence, applies genomics, single-cell and functional genomics analysis, and ML to target discovery, patient stratification and disease biology, including cancer. Prescient Design is a team of roughly 80 people, based largely in New York. It builds generative and ML models for designing and optimising antibodies and other large molecules, and its models are used in several preclinical programs.

entries.name: Eli Lilly
entries.focus: Lilly launched TuneLab on 2025-09-09. It is a federated AI/ML platform that gives smaller biotechs access to drug-discovery models trained on more than $1B of Lilly's internal R&D data. Biotechs can run the models on their own proprietary data without handing it over. Access is free for selected partners and sits within Lilly Catalyze360. Lilly plans to add in vivo small-molecule predictive models and NVIDIA Clara open-source model workflows. Separately, Lilly is building a large NVIDIA-powered AI supercomputer for its own discovery work. Public sources I found describe small-molecule and drug-discovery modelling. They do not mention cancer genomics or sequencing-based methods.

fit.reason: The public TuneLab and AI work centres on small-molecule and drug-discovery ML, which overlaps only through the student's ML-methods interest. The student's cancer genomics, structural variant and single-cell focus doesn't show up in it, and the open internship is US-based with unclear visa terms.

Internal research teams cover bioinformatics (including copy-number modelling), translational research on transcriptome and NGS data, and applied AI.

entries.name: Illumina
entries.focus: Illumina's AI lab builds deep-learning models that predict the effect of genetic variants. SpliceAI predicts splice-altering variants, PrimateAI-3D scores missense variants, and PromoterAI scores noncoding promoter variants. SpliceAI2 (October 2026) was trained on a dataset more than 100 times larger than the original, and Illumina reports it found 17% more disease-relevant variants on a rare-disease dataset. These tools aim to resolve variants of unknown significance in rare disease and to support drug target discovery. They are delivered through Illumina Connected Software and the Emedgene interpretation platform. The BioInsight business adds large multi-omic data assets and AI software for drug discovery.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with computational and ML methods for genomics and with variant and splicing analysis, but the team's focus is germline and rare-disease variant interpretation rather than cancer, somatic SVs or single-cell and spatial work, and US/UK roles would need work authorization.

entries.name: Recursion
entries.focus: Recursion runs an automated 'lab-in-the-loop' drug discovery platform. It generates very large cell-imaging (phenomics), transcriptomic and other perturbation datasets, and uses ML to map how genetic and chemical perturbations change cell state. Valence Labs, its AI research arm (formed in 2023 with the Valence Discovery acquisition, with sites in Montreal and London), works on three themes. 'Predict' models cell responses to perturbation, including multimodal and multi-omic foundation models. 'Explain' builds causal explanations of how molecular interventions affect cell function. 'Discover' uses lab-in-the-loop engines to generate and test therapeutic hypotheses. The company's clinical pipeline is largely oncology and rare disease, and it also publishes open models and datasets.

fit.reason: Single-cell ML and computational methods for genomics overlap with the student's interests, but Recursion focuses on perturbation phenomics and drug discovery rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis. Student programs are currently paused or have no openings.
